title: The arrow removed; Athena answers
intro: Pandarus mistakes a wound for victory. Diomedes gets the arrow removed and invokes Athena’s earlier relationship with his father. The exchange is especially useful for recovering epic imperatives and the various stems of familiar irregular verbs.

notes.text: δήθα means ‘for long.’ ἀνσχήσεσθαι is a future middle infinitive of ἀνέχω, with shortened ἀν- for ἀνα- and the σχ- stem seen in ἔσχον: ‘hold out against / endure.’ It depends on φημι from the preceding page, with Diomedes as accusative subject. ἐτεόν is adverbial ‘truly.’ Pandarus makes Apollo’s supposed support the condition of his prediction.

ἀπορνύμενον is present middle participle of ἀπόρνυμαι, ‘set out,’ agreeing with με. Λυκίηθεν uses the source suffix -θεν, ‘from Lycia.’ εὔχομαι can mean either ‘pray’ or ‘boast’: here εὐχόμενος characterizes Pandarus’ triumphant claim, while the same formula later introduces Diomedes’ prayer.

δάμασσεν is epic aorist of δαμάζω, ‘subdue’; the narrator directly denies the boast. ἀναχωρήσας is aorist participle, ‘having withdrawn.’ πρόσθεν governs genitive dual ἵπποιιν, ‘in front of his horses’; ὄχεσφιν is the parallel epic -φι form for the chariot. ἔστη is intransitive root-aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stood.’

ὄρσο is aorist middle imperative of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse yourself.’ καταβήσεο is an epic second-singular future middle used as a command, ‘you shall get down / get down.’ ὄφρα introduces purpose with ἐρύσσῃς, aorist active subjunctive of ἐρύω, ‘draw out.’ ὤμοιο is genitive singular in -οιο.

πέπον is a familiar affectionate address, ‘dear fellow,’ from πέπων; it is not a literal comment on ripeness. Καπανηϊάδη is vocative of the patronymic ‘son of Capaneus,’ identifying Sthenelus. Heroic companions often address one another through the father’s name, keeping family identity active in the scene.

ἆλτο is a root-aorist middle of ἅλλομαι, ‘leapt’; χαμᾶζε means ‘to the ground.’ στάς is root-aorist active participle of ἵστημι. ἐξέρυσε is aorist of ἐξερύω, ‘pulled out.’ διαμπερές emphasizes the arrow’s passage right through. ἀνηκόντιζε, imperfect of ἀνακοντίζω, depicts the blood spurting up through the woven tunic.

ἠρᾶτο is imperfect of ἀράομαι, ‘pray.’ κλῦθι is second-singular aorist imperative of κλύω, ‘hear’; μευ is epic genitive of ἐγώ, governed by hearing. The extra acute in κλῦθί comes from the enclitic. βοὴν ἀγαθός is an accusative of respect, ‘good at the war cry.’

αἰγίοχος describes Zeus as bearing the aegis; αἰγιόχοιο agrees with Διός. τέκος is a neuter vocative, ‘child.’ Ἀτρυτώνη is Athena’s title, conventionally understood as ‘unwearied.’ φῖλαι is aorist active imperative of φιλέω, ‘show me favour,’ not a plural noun. φίλα φρονέουσα means ‘thinking kindly,’ with φίλα used adverbially.

The prayer recalls previous assistance and requests its renewal: ‘if ever you stood beside me and my father … now favour me.’ παρέστης is second-singular intransitive aorist of παρίστημι. δός is aorist imperative of δίδωμι and governs ἑλεῖν and ἐλθεῖν, ‘grant [me] to kill … and come within spear-thrust.’

ἑλεῖν is second-aorist active infinitive of αἱρέω; ἐλθεῖν belongs to ἔρχομαι. φθάμενος is aorist middle participle of φθάνω, ‘getting in first’: Pandarus hit him before he could strike. ὄψεσθαι is future middle infinitive of ὁράω, ‘see,’ after φησι. φάος is the epic uncontracted noun ‘light’; seeing sunlight is a formula for being alive.

ἔκλυε is past indicative of κλύω, answering κλῦθι: Athena heard. ἔθηκεν is aorist of τίθημι, with object and predicate adjective, ‘made his limbs light.’ πόδας and χεῖρας specify the limbs; ὕπερθεν distinguishes the upper limbs. ἱσταμένη is present middle participle of ἵστημι, ‘taking her stand’ near him.

μάχεσθαι is a present middle infinitive used imperativally, ‘fight!’ θαρσῶν is the accompanying participle, ‘being confident.’ ἧκα is first singular aorist of ἵημι, ‘I put / sent,’ not ἥκω. πατρώϊον means inherited from the father. ἔχεσκε is an iterative past of ἔχω, ‘used to have’; σακέσπαλος, ‘shield-brandishing,’ and ἱππότα, an epic masculine nominative, characterize Tydeus.
